Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

[LLM] OP-512 C2 beacon to ashx.lhlsjcb[.]com from IIS host Command & Control High
Detects DNS resolutions or HTTP egress to the OP-512 attacker-controlled domain ashx.lhlsjcb[.]com observed in the ReliaQuest report. Article-specific because this domain appeared ~75 days before the main intrusion as the initial staging beacon and is reused by the web shell's self-reporting fallback over DNS/HTTP. Rationale: The domain ashx.lhlsjcb[.]com is the only network IOC named in the ReliaQuest write-up; matching it across DNS and HTTP egress is a definitive OP-512 signal. Cross-checked the IOC pattern via the article's lead and MITRE T1071.004 mapping. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteUrl has "lhlsjcb.com" or RemoteUrl has_cs "ashx.lhlsjcb.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp asc
let ioc_domain = "lhlsjcb.com";
(union isfuzzy=true
    (DnsEvents
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where Name has ioc_domain
        | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP, Domain = Name, QueryTypeName, Source = "DnsEvents"),
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where DnsQuery has ioc_domain
        | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DnsQuery, QueryTypeName = DnsQueryTypeName, Source = "ImDnsActivity"),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where RequestURL has ioc_domain or DestinationHostName has ioc_domain or DestinationDnsDomain has ioc_domain
        | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain), URL = RequestURL, Source = "CommonSecurityLog")
)
| order by TimeGenerated asc

[LLM] IIS worker w3wp.exe writes .aspx/.ashx handler to upload/temp directory (OP-512 web shell drop) Installation High
Detects the IIS worker process w3wp.exe writing ASP.NET handler files (.aspx, .ashx, .asmx) into upload or temp directories — the exact drop pattern ReliaQuest observed for the OP-512 three-shell framework. Combines parent-process (w3wp.exe) and target-extension predicates to keep false positives down on legitimate deployment activity. Rationale: ReliaQuest explicitly names w3wp.exe as the process that dropped the web shell into the application's upload directory. The parent (w3wp.exe) + extension (.aspx/.ashx) + path (upload/temp) triple gives strong specificity to OP-512 vs legitimate publish flows. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx" or FileName endswith ".asax"
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\upload", "\\uploads", "\\temp", "\\tmp", "\\App_Data", "\\images", "\\files")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RequestSourceIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "w3wp.exe"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx", "ashx", "asmx", "asax")
   or TargetFileName endswith ".aspx"
   or TargetFileName endswith ".ashx"
   or TargetFileName endswith ".asmx"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\upload", "\\uploads", "\\temp", "\\tmp", "\\App_Data", "\\images", "\\files")
| project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IIS w3wp.exe Writes ASP.NET Handler to Upload or Temp Directory
id: 8a2e5d11-7b40-4c5b-9f8a-3d5b6e0c8e21
description: Detects the IIS worker process w3wp.exe creating ASP.NET handler files (.aspx/.ashx/.asmx/.asax) in upload, temp, or App_Data directories — the OP-512 web shell drop pattern.
references:

logsource:

| ContextImageFileName=/\\w3wp\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(aspx|ashx|asmx|asax)$/i
| regex("\\\\(upload[s]?|temp|tmp|App_Data|images|files)\\\\", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp)])

[LLM] IIS w3wp.exe spawns whoami /priv or cmd.exe — OP-512 web shell command execution Actions on Objectives High
Detects the IIS worker w3wp.exe spawning interpreter or reconnaissance binaries (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, whoami.exe, net.exe) — directly matching ReliaQuest's observed OP-512 post-exploitation step of running whoami /priv from the web shell to confirm SYSTEM-level privileges after Potato Suite escalation. Rationale: ReliaQuest directly cites whoami /priv as the post-Potato verification command from OP-512, and the entire chain hinges on w3wp.exe being the parent. Parent (w3wp.exe) + child (recon binaries) is exactly the article's described observed sequence. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1033/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003 T1033 T1087
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "whoami.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "tasklist.exe", "hostname.exe", "wmic.exe", "reg.exe", "sc.exe")
| extend IsWhoamiPriv = (FileName =~ "whoami.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/priv", "/all", "/groups"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, IsWhoamiPriv
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ChildName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "whoami.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "tasklist.exe", "hostname.exe", "wmic.exe", "reg.exe", "sc.exe")
| extend IsWhoamiPriv = (ChildName =~ "whoami.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("/priv", "/all", "/groups"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType, IsWhoamiPriv
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] OP-512 Potato Suite SYSTEM escalation from IIS worker (SeImpersonate token abuse) Exploitation High
Detects token-impersonation privilege escalation from the IIS app-pool identity to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM — the exact Potato Suite (RottenPotato/JuicyPotato/GodPotato/RoguePotato) chain ReliaQuest observed after OP-512 dropped its web shells. Pivots on child of w3wp.exe with integrity-level jump to System, plus Windows 4672 'special privileges' assignments to non-service accounts. Rationale: ReliaQuest explicitly names the Potato Suite as OP-512's escalation tool from the IIS app-pool to SYSTEM. The IIS-worker-as-parent plus Potato binary-name keywords plus integrity-level jump make this a high-fidelity escalation indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001/ • https://github.com/ohpe/juicy-potato • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/
ATT&CKT1134.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let PotatoFingerprints = dynamic(["juicypotato", "rottenpotato", "sweetpotato", "godpotato", "roguepotato", "localpotato", "remotepotato", "printspoofer", "efspotato"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in~ ("System", "High")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (PotatoFingerprints)
   or FileName has_any (PotatoFingerprints)
   or InitiatingProcessTokenElevation =~ "TokenElevationTypeFull" and AccountName =~ "SYSTEM" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system", "network service", "local service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, ProcessTokenElevation, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
let PotatoNames = dynamic(["juicypotato", "rottenpotato", "sweetpotato", "godpotato", "roguepotato", "localpotato", "remotepotato", "printspoofer", "efspotato"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| extend ChildName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where TokenElevationType in ("%%1936", "%%1937")  // Full or Default-elevated
   or CommandLine has_any (PotatoNames)
   or ChildName has_any (PotatoNames)
   or (SubjectUserSid == "S-1-5-18" and ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectUserSid, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

Hackers Exploit Critical Everest Forms Pro WordPress Plugin Flaw to Take Over Sites

The Hacker News
2026-06-05 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical security flaw in Everest Forms Pro, a WordPress plugin with about 4,000 active installations, to execute arbitrary code, leading to a complete site compromise. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-3300 (CVSS score: 9.8), a remote code execution bug impacting all versions of the plugin up to, and including, 1.9.12. A patch for the flaw was

[LLM] Everest Forms Pro RCE exploit attempt from named source IPs Delivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to vulnerable WordPress sites from the four IPv4 sources Wordfence attributed to the CVE-2026-3300 exploitation campaign. Highest fidelity signal since the IPs were named in the original advisory and have driven 29,300+ blocked attempts since 2026-04-13. Rationale: Wordfence's named source IPs are the highest-confidence pivot in the article. Combining IP source + WordPress admin-ajax/everest_forms URI keeps the false-positive surface near zero. Cross-checked with Wordfence's advisory and abuse.ch ThreatFox for IP reputation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wordfence.com/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/

[LLM] Everest Forms Pro Calculation Addon PHP injection payload in form submission Exploitation Medium
Hunts POST bodies to WordPress endpoints containing PHP code-context characters that escape sanitize_text_field() and reach eval() in process_filter(). Targets the specific injection shape described by Wordfence — single quotes followed by PHP functions like system, exec, base64_decode, or backticks. Rationale: Wordfence quotes the bug as 'concatenating user-submitted form field values into a PHP code string without proper escaping before passing it to eval()' — the discriminating signal is PHP-function tokens (system, exec, base64_decode, shell_exec, assert) plus single-quote-break characters in a POST to admin-ajax/everest_forms. Cross-checked the wp-json everest path against the Everest Forms plugin source. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wordfence.com/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004

[LLM] WordPress rogue 'diksimarina' admin account creation request Installation High
Hunts the specific payload Wordfence saw most commonly in CVE-2026-3300 exploitation: creation of a WordPress administrator account named 'diksimarina' with email 'diksimarina@gmail.com'. Rationale: 'diksimarina' and 'diksimarina@gmail.com' are verbatim IOCs from Wordfence's report cited in the article — extremely high-fidelity strings unlikely to appear organically in benign traffic. Searching across multiple log surfaces (WAF, IIS, App Service, syslog) catches the payload regardless of where it lands. [LLM] WordPress PHP worker spawning shell or download utility post-RCE Installation Medium
Hunts the post-exploit behaviour where the PHP/Apache/Nginx worker process spawns sh, bash, wget, curl, python, perl, or nc — the natural follow-on after process_filter() eval() succeeds and the attacker drops a webshell or pulls a second-stage payload. Rationale: The article's kill-chain note explicitly cites 'PHP/Apache/Nginx worker processes spawning unusual children (sh, curl, wget)' as the execution-phase pivot. Pairing the parent web-tier binary with download/shell child binaries follows the BluRaven process-tree pattern and avoids the anti-bare-process-execution smell. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003 T1105

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-3300")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-3300")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] GHOST STADIUM FIFA lookalike domain resolution (fifa.bio/.center/.gold/.red/.sale/.shopping/.show/.ski) · [LLM] GHOST STADIUM PingIdentity SSO clone: external referrer hot-linking fifa.com static assets · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Massiv / Perseus (Cerberus-derived) Android banking trojan APK hash on managed endpoint · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GHOST STADIUM phishing kit / Android trojan C2 IP egress (8 specific hosts) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] GHOST STADIUM FIFA lookalike domain resolution (fifa.bio/.center/.gold/.red/.sale/.shopping/.show/.ski) Delivery High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP connection from corporate or employee endpoints to the specific FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike domains attributed to GHOST STADIUM. Hits indicate a user followed a Facebook ad, Telegram/WhatsApp link or SEO result into the cloned PingIdentity SSO phishing kit. Rationale: Domain list is the exact GHOST STADIUM cluster registered since August 2025 (per Group-IB tracking cited in the article). These are not legitimate FIFA properties — fifa.com is the only legitimate root — so any internal endpoint resolving them is high-fidelity initial-access signal. Cross-checked against the kill-chain Phase 1 IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html

[LLM] GHOST STADIUM phishing kit / Android trojan C2 IP egress (8 specific hosts) Command & Control High
Detects outbound connections from any internal endpoint (workstation, mobile via NAT, server) to the eight IP addresses that host the cloned fifa.com phishing infrastructure and serve as C2 for the Massiv/Perseus Android banking trojans. Article-specific IP set, not a reputation feed. Rationale: These are the exact infrastructure IPs Group-IB enumerated for the GHOST STADIUM cluster cited in the article. Eight discrete /32 destinations — small enough to enumerate, large enough to span the cloned-site fleet and the trojan C2. Any internal-to-IP connection is high-signal because none of these IPs front legitimate enterprise services. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html

[LLM] Massiv / Perseus (Cerberus-derived) Android banking trojan APK hash on managed endpoint Installation High
Detects the three specific SHA1 hashes of the trojanised RojaDirecta-style streaming APKs distributed alongside the World Cup 2026 fraud campaign. Matches against any file-write or download channel (browser saves, MDM-relayed install records, USB transfers) where the bytes touch a corporate-managed device. Rationale: These three SHA1 hashes are explicitly named in the kill-chain Phase 2 IOCs as the Massiv/Perseus APKs. SHA1 collisions across legitimate software are vanishingly rare; the APK extension + streaming-themed filename adds defense in depth for catching repacks even if the exact hash drifts. Highest-confidence host-side signal in the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1660 T1626.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA1 in (MassivPerseusHashes) or (FileName endswith ".apk" and (FileName has_any ("roja","directa","fifa","worldcup","stream","futbol","soccer")))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, FileOriginIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let MassivPerseusHashes = dynamic(["3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1","84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c","9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA1 in (MassivPerseusHashes)
   or (TargetFileExtension =~ "apk" and TargetFileName has_any ("roja","directa","fifa","worldcup","stream","futbol","soccer"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256

[LLM] GHOST STADIUM PingIdentity SSO clone: external referrer hot-linking fifa.com static assets Delivery Medium
Detects the signature visual-evasion technique of the GHOST STADIUM phishing kit — the cloned login page hot-links images directly from fifa.com so that brand-similarity scanners see the assets as legitimate. Hunts for outbound requests to fifa.com static-asset paths whose Referer header is NOT a fifa.com hostname. Rationale: The article explicitly describes this evasion: "It loads its images straight from FIFA's own servers, so the page looks authentic and slips past tools that flag copied images." Hot-linking inverts the normal Referer relationship — a phishing page loads fifa.com/<asset> with its own non-fifa hostname in the Referer header. Whitelisting fifa.com itself, PingIdentity (the real SSO provider), and search engines isolates the phishing-kit traffic shape. This is the rare detection that catches the kit's structural choice, not just the rotating IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html
ATT&CKT1656 T1036.005 T1608.005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","HttpConnectionInspected")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend RemoteUrlLower = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrlLower has "fifa.com"
| where RemoteUrlLower matches regex @"fifa\.com/.+\.(jpg|jpeg|png|svg|webp|gif|css)(\?|$)"
   or RemoteUrlLower has_any ("fifa.com/assets/","fifa.com/static/","fifa.com/images/","fifa.com/_next/")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "BrowserLaunchedToOpenUrl" or AdditionalFields has "Referrer"
    | extend Referrer = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).Referrer)
    | where isnotempty(Referrer) and Referrer !contains "fifa.com" and Referrer !contains "pingidentity.com"
    | project DeviceId, RefTime=Timestamp, Referrer
  ) on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (RefTime .. RefTime + 30s)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Referrer, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let LegitimateReferrers = dynamic(["fifa.com","www.fifa.com","pingidentity.com","ping.fifa.com","fifa.tm","ticketing.fifa.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)fifa\.com/.+\.(jpg|jpeg|png|svg|webp|gif|css)(\?|$)"
   or Url has_any ("fifa.com/assets/","fifa.com/static/","fifa.com/images/","fifa.com/_next/")
| extend ReferrerHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(HttpRequestHeaderReferer).Host))
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderReferer)
| where not (ReferrerHost in (LegitimateReferrers))
| where not (ReferrerHost endswith ".fifa.com")
| where ReferrerHost !has "google." and ReferrerHost !has "bing." and ReferrerHost !has "duckduckgo."
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, ReferrerHost, Url, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

status: experimental
description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or SHA1 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or MD5 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or SHA1 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or MD5 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Cisco SD-WAN Manager CVE-2026-20245 exploitation via vconfd tenant-list upload
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Cisco warns of unpatched SD-WAN zero-day exploited in attacks
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Cisco SD-WAN Manager CVE-2026-20245 exploitation via vconfd tenant-list upload Exploitation High
Hunts the literal Mandiant/Cisco PSIRT IOC published for CVE-2026-20245: the vScript daemon on Catalyst SD-WAN Manager (formerly vManage) logging a 'Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number' event in /var/log/scripts.log that invokes /usr/bin/vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh with an attacker-controlled -cli path argument. A successful exploit yields root via command injection in the tenant-list parser; the attacker must already hold netadmin (chained from CVE-2026-20182 or CVE-2026-20127), so any hit warrants immediate investigation of preceding admin-tier auth. Rationale: Anchors on three verbatim strings from the Cisco PSIRT example log line: the vScript syslog tag, the literal phrase 'Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number', and the path /usr/bin/vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh. All three appearing together on the same record is the exact IOC Cisco told customers to grep for in /var/log/scripts.log. The extracted -cli path argument is exposed for triage so analysts can immediately judge whether the uploaded file sits in a sane tenant-config directory or in /home, /tmp etc. (the malicious.csv example sits in /home/admin). Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch are empty because vManage is a Cisco appliance, not an EDR-managed endpoint or AWS resource. No external corroboration sought — the article reproduces the vendor advisory IOC verbatim and the CVE is too fresh (June 2026) for second-source IOC bundles to exist yet.
ATT&CKT1190 T1068 T1059.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "vScript"
    and SyslogMessage has "Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number"
    and SyslogMessage has "vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh"
| extend UploadPath = extract(@"-cli\s+path\s+(\S+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend VpnId = extract(@"vpn\s+(\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend SuspiciousPath = iff(UploadPath matches regex @"^/(home|tmp|var/tmp|dev/shm)/", "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, UploadPath, VpnId, SuspiciousPath, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager CVE-2026-20245 Exploitation via vconfd Tenant Upload
id: 7c4e8d9a-2f5b-4c1d-8e6a-9b2c3d4e5f60
status: experimental
description: |
  Detects exploitation of Cisco SD-WAN Manager CVE-2026-20245 via the
  vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh helper, where an attacker holding
  netadmin privileges uploads a crafted tenant-list file to achieve root
  command injection. Anchors on the literal /var/log/scripts.log artefact
  published by Cisco PSIRT.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-cisco-sd-wan-flaw-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks-to-gain-root/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/05
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.privilege_escalation
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: syslog
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Message|contains: 'vScript'
  selection_pattern:
    Message|contains|all:
      - 'Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number'
      - 'vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh'
      - '-cli path'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_pattern
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate tenant onboarding executed by trusted operators (validate -cli path argument and operator session)
level: high
source:linux.syslog "vScript" "Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number" "vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh" "-cli path"
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Changes.command) as commands values(All_Changes.object) as objects values(All_Changes.user) as users from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.dest_type IN ("network","appliance") AND All_Changes.command="*vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh*" AND All_Changes.command="*Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number*" by All_Changes.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)`
| rex field=commands "-cli\s+path\s+(?<upload_path>\S+)"
| rex field=commands "vpn\s+(?<vpn_id>\d+)"
| eval suspicious_path=if(match(upload_path,"^/(home|tmp|var/tmp|dev/shm)/"),"yes","no")
| where isnotnull(upload_path)
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| table firstTime lastTime dest users upload_path vpn_id suspicious_path count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Changes.command) as commands values(All_Changes.object) as objects values(All_Changes.user) as users from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.dest_type IN ("network","appliance") AND All_Changes.command="*vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh*" AND All_Changes.command="*Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number*" by All_Changes.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)`
| rex field=commands "-cli\s+path\s+(?<upload_path>\S+)"
| rex field=commands "vpn\s+(?<vpn_id>\d+)"
| eval suspicious_path=if(match(upload_path,"^/(home|tmp|var/tmp|dev/shm)/"),"yes","no")
| where isnotnull(upload_path)
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| table firstTime lastTime dest users upload_path vpn_id suspicious_path count
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20245", "CVE-2026-20182", "CVE-2026-20127", "CVE-2026-20133", "CVE-2026-20128", "CVE-2026-20122")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20245", "CVE-2026-20182", "CVE-2026-20127", "CVE-2026-20133", "CVE-2026-20128", "CVE-2026-20122")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-20245", "CVE-2026-20182", "CVE-2026-20127", "CVE-2026-20133", "CVE-2026-20128", "CVE-2026-20122")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-20245", "CVE-2026-20182", "CVE-2026-20127", "CVE-2026-20133", "CVE-2026-20128", "CVE-2026-20122")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PCPJack Hijacks 230 AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure Servers for Covert SMTP Relay Network

The Hacker News
2026-06-05 14 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actor known as PCPJack has hijacked cloud servers associated with Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure to create a covert SMTP email relay network. "Compromised business servers across the U.S., Europe, and Asia were quietly converted into SMTP proxies, verified for mail relay capability, and synced to a downstream consumer every five minutes," Hunt.io said in

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — PCPJack Hijacks 230 AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure Servers for Covert SMTP Relay N
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PCPJack hidden Chisel implant drop at /var/tmp/.xs on Linux
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PCPJack Sliver server 213.136.80.73 (esp. port 9000) · [LLM] PCPJack SOCKS5 listener bound to deterministic port 10000-14999 on Linux · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PCPJack SMTP quality-gate probe to smtp.gmail.com:587 from non-mail Linux workloads · [LLM] SCP exfiltration of PCPJack proxy lists to downstream collector 38.242.204.245 · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Outbound C2 to PCPJack Sliver server 213.136.80.73 (esp. port 9000) Command & Control High
Detect any host beaconing to the PCPJack Sliver C2 IP 213.136.80.73 — particularly the port 9000 health-check the diagnostic script polls and the SCP/SSH (22) and HTTPS callbacks beacons use. Highest-confidence indicator in the article: the C2 IP itself was confirmed open and live by Hunt.io. Rationale: 213.136.80.73 is the unauthenticated PCPJack C2 server Hunt.io confirmed live with ports 8444/9443/9000 exposed; pivoting on the IP alone is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Hunt.io's write-up and the prior SentinelOne PCPJack analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/cloud-worm-evicts-teampcp-and-steals-credentials-at-scale/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "213.136.80.73"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| extend Port9000Health = iif(RemotePort == 9000, "yes", "no")
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP == "213.136.80.73"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "213.136.80.73"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetProto=NetworkProtocol, EventVendor, EventProduct, DvcAction)
| extend Port9000Health = iif(DstPort == 9000, "yes", "no")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PCPJack SMTP quality-gate probe to smtp.gmail.com:587 from non-mail Linux workloads Actions on Objectives High
Hunt for the Sliver deployer's outbound 'mail relay capability' probe to smtp.gmail.com:587, which the script uses to filter beacons worth keeping. A cloud VM (AWS/GCP/Azure) opening port 587 to gmail from a non-mail workload is a sharp PCPJack-specific signal. Rationale: The article's SMTP quality gate is literally a TCP 587 probe to smtp.gmail.com — extremely specific behaviour for a non-mail workload. Confirmed by Hunt.io's primary source. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1090 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 587
| where RemoteUrl =~ "smtp.gmail.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".gmail.com"
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["mailrelay01","mailrelay02"]))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DestinationPort == 587
  | where DestinationHostName has "smtp.gmail.com" or DestinationDnsDomain has "gmail.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DstPortNumber == 587
  | where DstHostname has "smtp.gmail.com" or DstDomain has "gmail.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstHost=DstHostname, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetProto=NetworkProtocol)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] SCP exfiltration of PCPJack proxy lists to downstream collector 38.242.204.245 Actions on Objectives High
PCPJack syncs the verified-proxy list every five minutes via SCP to 38.242.204.245. Hunt for SSH/SCP/rsync connections to this IP, or process events showing scp/sftp invoking this destination on Linux beacons. Rationale: 38.242.204.245 is the named downstream collector receiving five-minute SCP syncs; pairing the IP with scp/rsync command-line keeps FP low. Confirmed by Hunt.io. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteIP == "38.242.204.245"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType),
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("scp","sftp","rsync","sshpass","ssh")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "38.242.204.245"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP == "38.242.204.245"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "38.242.204.245"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("scp","sftp","rsync","sshpass")
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "38.242.204.245"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PCPJack hidden Chisel implant drop at /var/tmp/.xs on Linux Installation High
On the victim side the Sliver/Chisel binary is dropped as the hidden dot-prefixed file /var/tmp/.xs. Detect creation of this exact path, or any executable written to /var/tmp/ whose name starts with '.', then chmod'd +x. Rationale: /var/tmp/.xs is an exact path called out in the article as the persistence location for the Sliver/Chisel binary. Filtering well-known dot dirs keeps FPs minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/"
| where FileName startswith "." and FileName !in~ (".X11-unix",".ICE-unix",".font-unix")
| extend IsXs = iif(FolderPath == "/var/tmp/.xs" or FileName == ".xs", "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, IsXs
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/var/tmp/"
| where TargetFileName startswith "." and TargetFileName !in~ (".X11-unix",".ICE-unix",".font-unix")
| extend IsXs = iif(TargetFilePath == "/var/tmp/.xs" or TargetFileName == ".xs", "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, IsXs
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PCPJack SOCKS5 listener bound to deterministic port 10000-14999 on Linux Command & Control Medium
The deployer derives each beacon's SOCKS5 proxy port from an MD5 of its Sliver UUID, mapped to 10000-14999. Hunt for newly-bound listeners in that port range on Linux servers, especially when the listener is a non-standard binary in /var/tmp or /tmp. Rationale: The 10000-14999 SOCKS5 port range is explicitly called out and derived from MD5(UUID); restricting to listeners spawned from /var/tmp or /tmp narrows it to PCPJack-likely cases. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1090.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ListeningConnectionCreated","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| where LocalPort between (10000 .. 14999)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "."
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection in ("Inbound","Listen")
| where SrcPortNumber between (10000 .. 14999) or DstPortNumber between (10000 .. 14999)
| extend Port = coalesce(SrcPortNumber, DstPortNumber)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), DistinctPorts=dcount(Port), PortList=make_set(Port,50), Connections=count() by DvcHostname, EventVendor, EventProduct
| where DistinctPorts >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @SourcePort:[10000 TO 14999]) OR (source:linux.auditd @network.client.port:[10000 TO 14999] @process.executable.path:(\/var\/tmp\/* OR \/tmp\/.*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkListenIP4 LocalPort>=10000 LocalPort<=14999
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(var\/)?tmp\//i OR ContextImageFileName=/\/\.[^\/]+$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, LocalPort], function=count())
